label: def:dynkin
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:dynkin}
The integer $j(\varphi)$ of \eqref{eq:dynkinpullback} is the \emph{Dynkin index} of $\varphi$. The Dynkin index $j(\mathfrak{s})$ of a simple subalgebra $\mathfrak{s} \subset \mathfrak{g}$ is the Dynkin index of the inclusion $\mathfrak{s} \hookrightarrow \mathfrak{g}$. The Dynkin index $\ell_{\rho}$ of a nonzero representation $\rho:\mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(V)$ is the Dynkin index of $\rho$ regarded as a homomorphism $\mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{sl}(V)$.

label: lem:dynkinformula
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the diagonal Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{sl}(n, \mathbb C)$ and the root $\alpha = \epsilon_{a} - \epsilon_{b}$, $a \neq b$, where $\epsilon_{a}(H) = H_{aa}$, the element $t = E_{aa} - E_{bb}$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(tH) = \alpha(H)$ for diagonal $H$, so the length of $\alpha$ for the form $\operatorname{tr} XY$ is $(\alpha, \alpha) = \operatorname{tr} t^{2} = 2$. All roots of $\mathfrak{sl}(n, \mathbb C)$ are long, so $\operatorname{tr} XY$ is the normalized form, and \eqref{eq:repindex} is \eqref{eq:dynkinpullback} for $\rho:\mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{sl}(V)$. This shows \ref{dynkinformula1}.

The linear map $\varphi:\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C) \to \mathfrak{s}$ sending $E_{12}$, $E_{21}$, $E_{11} - E_{22}$ to $e$, $f$, $h$ is an isomorphism of Lie algebras by \eqref{eq:sl2triple}, and $j(\mathfrak{s})$ is the Dynkin index of the composition of $\varphi$ with the inclusion $\mathfrak{s} \hookrightarrow \mathfrak{g}$, because $\varphi$ preserves normalized forms. By \ref{dynkinformula1} and \eqref{eq:dynkinpullback}, $(h, h) = j(\mathfrak{s})\operatorname{tr}(E_{11} - E_{22})^{2} = 2j(\mathfrak{s})$, and $B(h, h) = 2h^\vee(h, h)$ by \eqref{eq:Bnorm}. This shows \ref{dynkinformula2}.

body_md:
Because $\tau\mathfrak{s} = \mathfrak{s}$, $\mathfrak{s} = \mathfrak{s}_{0} \oplus i\mathfrak{s}_{0}$, and $-B$ is a positive definite invariant inner product on $\mathfrak{s}_{0}$, so $\mathfrak{s}_{0}$ is a three-dimensional compact semisimple Lie algebra, hence isomorphic to $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, which has a basis satisfying the first relations of \eqref{eq:xirelations}. By invariance, for $(a, b, c)$ a cyclic permutation of $(1, 2, 3)$, $B(z_{a}, z_{a}) = B(z_{a}, [z_{b}, z_{c}]) = B([z_{a}, z_{b}], z_{c}) = B(z_{c}, z_{c})$ and $B(z_{a}, z_{b}) = B(z_{a}, [z_{c}, z_{a}]) = 0$, so $B(z_{a}, z_{b}) = -\beta'\delta_{ab}$ for some $\beta' > 0$. The triple relations \eqref{eq:sl2triple} for $(z_{1} + iz_{2}, -z_{1} + iz_{2}, 2iz_{3})$ are direct computations from \eqref{eq:xirelations}, and $\tau$ acts on them as stated because $\tau z_{a} = z_{a}$. Since $B(2iz_{3}, 2iz_{3}) = 4\beta'$, \eqref{eq:dynkinindex} gives $\beta' = jh^\vee = \beta$.

For \ref{sl2b}, in the coordinates $x = \sum_{a=1}^{3}x_{a}z_{a}$, $y = \sum_{a=1}^{3}y_{a}z_{a}$, the bracket is the complex bilinear cross product of the coefficient vectors and $H$ is $\beta$ times the standard Hermitian product, so \eqref{eq:sl2norm} is $\beta$ times the Lagrange identity $|x \times y|^{2} = |x|^{2}|y|^{2} - |x \cdot \bar{y}|^{2}$.

label: lem:lower
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:lower}
\leavevmode\noindent
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*), ref=(\arabic*)]
\item\label{lower1} Every subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}$ isomorphic to $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$ is conjugate under the adjoint group to a $\tau$-stable subalgebra.
\item\label{lower2} Let $0 \neq e \in \mathfrak{g}_{\theta}$ with $\lVert e\rVert^{2} = 2h^\vee$, and put $f := -\tau e$ and $h := \theta^{\vee}$. Then $(e, f, h)$ is an $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$-triple spanning the $\tau$-stable root subalgebra $\mathfrak{s}_{\theta}$ of \eqref{eq:rootsubalgebra}, which has Dynkin index $1$, $H(e, f) = 0$, and $\lVert [e, f]\rVert^{2} = \lVert e\rVert^{2}\lVert f\rVert^{2}/h^\vee$.
\item\label{lower3} Every $\tau$-stable subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}$ isomorphic to $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$ and having Dynkin index $1$ is $\operatorname{Ad}(G_{0})$-conjugate to $\mathfrak{s}_{\theta}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{lower1} Let $\mathfrak{s} \simeq \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$ and let $\mathfrak{s}_{c}$ be a compact real form of $\mathfrak{s}$. The analytic subgroup $S_{c}$ of the adjoint group $G$ of $\mathfrak{g}$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{s}_{c}$ is compact, being the image of $SU(2)$. The analytic subgroup $G_{0}$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}_{0}$ is a maximal compact subgroup of $G$, every compact subgroup of $G$ is contained in a maximal compact subgroup, and the maximal compact subgroups of $G$ are conjugate \cite[Chapter VI]{Helgason}, so $gS_{c}g^{-1} \subset G_{0}$ for some $g \in G$. Then $\operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak{s}_{c} \subset \mathfrak{g}_{0}$, and $\operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak{s} = \operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak{s}_{c} \oplus i\operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak{s}_{c}$ is $\tau$-stable.

\ref{lower2} By \eqref{eq:tauroot}, $f \in \mathfrak{g}_{-\theta}$, and $B(e, f) = -B(e, \tau e) = \lVert e\rVert^{2} = 2h^\vee$, so by \ref{R2} and $t_{\theta} = \theta^{\vee}/(2h^\vee)$, $[e, f] = \theta^{\vee} = h$. Since $\theta(\theta^{\vee}) = 2$, $(e, f, h)$ is an $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$-triple, and $\tau f = -\tau\tau e = -e$ and $\tau h = [\tau e, \tau f] = [-f, -e] = -h$, so its span is $\tau$-stable; by \eqref{eq:dynkinindex} its Dynkin index is $(\theta^{\vee}, \theta^{\vee})/2 = 1$. By \ref{R2}, $H(e, f) = -B(e, \tau f) = B(e, e) = 0$, and \eqref{eq:sl2norm} with $\beta = h^\vee$ gives the last claim.

\ref{lower3} Let $\mathfrak{s}$ be $\tau$-stable of Dynkin index $1$, let $z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}$ be as in Lemma \ref{lem:sl2str}\ref{sl2a}, and let $(e, f, h) = (z_{1} + iz_{2}, -z_{1} + iz_{2}, 2iz_{3})$. Since $z_{3} \in \mathfrak{g}_{0}$ is $\operatorname{Ad}(G_{0})$-conjugate into $\mathfrak{t}_{0}$, it can be assumed that $h \in i\mathfrak{t}_{0} \subset \mathfrak{h}$. The roots take integer values on $h$, because these are eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}(h)$, so $h$ lies in the real span of the coroots, and since the Weyl group is realized by the normalizer of $\mathfrak{t}_{0}$ in $G_{0}$, $h$ can be assumed dominant. As $j(\mathfrak{s}) = 1$, $(h, h) = 2$ by \eqref{eq:dynkinindex}, and the equality case in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:Bh} gives $h = \theta^{\vee}$, $e \in \mathfrak{g}_{\theta}$, and $f \in \mathfrak{g}_{-\theta}$, so $\mathfrak{s} = \mathfrak{s}_{\theta}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Bilinearity and commutativity are evident from \eqref{nahmproduct}. By \eqref{nahmproduct} and the cyclic invariance of $\omega$,
\begin{align}\label{eq:polarizationproof}
B(a \circledcirc b, c) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_{3}}\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)\omega(a_{\sigma(1)}, b_{\sigma(2)}, c_{\sigma(3)}),
\end{align}
where $S_{3}$ is the symmetric group and $\operatorname{sign}:S_{3}\to \{\pm 1\}$ the sign representation, and this equals the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:polarization} by the trilinearity of $\omega$.
This proves \eqref{eq:polarization} and \ref{nahm1}. The formula for $a \circledcirc a$ is \eqref{nahmproduct}, and \eqref{eq:derivativesC} follows from \eqref{eq:polarization}, since the derivatives of the cubic form $C$ are given by its polarization. Because $\tau$ is a conjugate-linear order $2$ automorphism of $\mathfrak{g}$, \eqref{nahmproduct} gives $\tau(a \circledcirc b) = \tau a \circledcirc \tau b$. By \ref{nahm1}, $H(a \circledcirc b, c) = -B(a \circledcirc b, \tau c) = -B(b, a \circledcirc \tau c) = -B(b, \tau(\tau a \circledcirc c)) = H(b, \tau a \circledcirc c)$. This shows \ref{nahm3}.
Finally, by \eqref{nahmproduct} the $i$th component of $\mathsf{L}(a)b$ does not depend on $b_{i}$, so $\mathsf{L}(a)$ has vanishing diagonal blocks and hence has trace zero. This shows \ref{nahm4}.

body_md:
Note that $U_{e}$ is the real tangent space at $e$ of the orbit $(\mathbb C^{\ast})^{3}\cdot e$ and consequently $JU_{e} = U_{e}$. That $U^{\perp}_{e}$ is the orthogonal complement of $U_{e}$ with respect to $\operatorname{Re} H$, follows from $H(b_{i}, e_{i}) = \operatorname{Re} H(b, \hat{e}_{i}) + i\operatorname{Re} H(b, J\hat{e}_{i})$, which shows that $U^{\perp}_{e} = \{b \in \mathfrak{g}^{3}: \operatorname{Re} H(b_{i}, e_{i}) = 0 = \operatorname{Re} H(b_{i}, Je_{i}) \text{ for } i \in \{1, 2, 3\}\}$, from which there follows $JU^{\perp}_{e} = U^{\perp}_{e}$ because $\operatorname{Re} H(Jb_{i}, e_{i}) = - \operatorname{Re} H(b_{i}, Je_{i})$.

By the invariance of $B$ with respect to $\circledcirc$ (Lemma \ref{lem:nahmbasic}\ref{nahm1}) and the commutativity of $\circledcirc$, $\operatorname{Re} H(a, \tau\mathsf{L}(e)b) = -\operatorname{Re} B(a, e \circledcirc b) = -\operatorname{Re} B(a\circledcirc b, e)$ is symmetric in $a$ and $b$, so $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)$ is self-adjoint with respect to $\operatorname{Re} H$.

By \eqref{nahmproduct} and $e \circledcirc e = \tau e$, $e \circledcirc \hat{e}_{1} = (0, [e_{3}, e_{1}], [e_{1}, e_{2}]) = \tfrac{1}{2}(0, \tau e_{2}, \tau e_{3})$, and applying $\tau$ gives $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)\hat{e}_{1} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{e}_{2} + \hat{e}_{3})$. Since $\mathsf{L}(e)$ is complex linear and $\tau$ is conjugate-linear, $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)J = -J\tau\mathsf{L}(e)$. Together with the preceding this implies $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)J\hat{e}_{1} = -\tfrac{1}{2}(J\hat{e}_{2} + J\hat{e}_{3})$. The same computations for $\hat{e}_{2}$ and $\hat{e}_{3}$ show that
\begin{align}\label{idem4}
&\tau\mathsf{L}(e)\hat{e}_{i} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{e}_{j} + \hat{e}_{k}), && \tau\mathsf{L}(e)J\hat{e}_{i} = -\tfrac{1}{2}(J\hat{e}_{j} + J\hat{e}_{k})
\end{align}
for $\{i, j, k\}$ a permutation of $\{1, 2, 3\}$. From \eqref{idem4} it follows that $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)U_{e} \subset U_{e}$ and, moreover, that the restriction of $\tau \mathsf{L}(e)$ to $U_{e}$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\pm 1$, each with multiplicity $1$, and $\pm 1/2$, each with multiplicity $2$, so that $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)U_{e} = U_{e}$.
Finally, $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)U^{\perp}_{e} \subset U^{\perp}_{e}$ follows from $\tau \mathsf{L}(e)U_{e} = U_{e}$ by the self-adjointness of $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)$ and nondegeneracy of $\operatorname{Re} H$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $e$ be a $\tau$-twisted idempotent at which $W$ attains its maximum, and let $j(\mathfrak{s}_{e})$ be the Dynkin index of the subalgebra $\mathfrak{s}_{e} = \operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb C}\{e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}\}$ of Lemma \ref{lem:rigidity}. By \eqref{eq:idemnorms}, $e_{1}, e_{2} \in \mathfrak{s}_{e}$ are nonzero and $H$-orthogonal, and $F(e_{1}, e_{2}) = W(e) = \lVert \omega\rVert_{\ast}^{2}$, while by \eqref{eq:sl2norm} applied to $e_{1}, e_{2}$, $F(e_{1}, e_{2}) = 1/(j(\mathfrak{s}_{e})h^\vee)$, so that $1/(j(\mathfrak{s}_{e})h^\vee) = \lVert \omega\rVert_{\ast}^{2}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:Bh}, $j(\mathfrak{s}_{e}) \geq 1$, while by  \eqref{eq:lowerbound}, $\frac{1}{h^\vee} \leq\lVert \omega\rVert_{\ast}^{2}$, so that
\begin{align}\label{eq:sharpchain}
\frac{1}{h^\vee} \leq \lVert \omega\rVert_{\ast}^{2} = \frac{1}{j(\mathfrak{s}_{e})h^\vee} \leq \frac{1}{h^\vee}.
\end{align}
By \eqref{eq:sharpchain}, $\lVert \omega\rVert_{\ast}^{2} = 1/h^\vee$ and $j(\mathfrak{s}_{e}) = 1$. This proves \eqref{eq:main}, by Lemma \ref{fkwmaxlemma}, and its optimality. It also shows that for every $\tau$-twisted idempotent $e$ at which $W$ attains its maximum, the components of $e$ span a $\tau$-stable subalgebra isomorphic to $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$ and having Dynkin index $1$.

Theorem \ref{thm:C}\ref{thmC1} is Lemma \ref{thm:idem}\ref{idem2},\ref{idem1}. For Theorem \ref{thm:C}\ref{thmC2}, a nonzero $\tau$-twisted idempotent $e$ satisfies $3/(4H(e, e)) = W(e) \leq \lVert \omega\rVert_{\ast}^{2} = 1/h^\vee$ by \eqref{eq:idemnorms}, with equality if and only if $W$ attains its maximum at $e$, in which case the components of $e$ span a $\tau$-stable subalgebra of Dynkin index $1$, as just shown. Conversely, if the components of $e$ span such a subalgebra $\mathfrak{s}$, then by \eqref{eq:idemnorms} and \eqref{eq:sl2norm} applied to the orthogonal pair $e_{1}, e_{2}$, $W(e) = F(e_{1}, e_{2}) = 1/h^\vee$.

For the equality case of Theorem \ref{thm:A}, let $p, q \neq 0$ satisfy $F(p, q) = 1/h^\vee$. Then $[p, q] \neq 0$ and $W(p, q, \tau[p, q]) = F(p, q) = \lVert \omega\rVert_{\ast}^{2}$ by Lemma \ref{fkwmaxlemma}\ref{fkw2}, so $(p, q, \tau[p, q]) \in \mathrm{Crit}^*(W)$. By Lemma \ref{thm:idem}\ref{idem1}, there is $c \in (\mathbb C^{\ast})^{3}$ such that the rescaling $e = c \cdot (p, q, \tau[p, q])$ is a $\tau$-twisted idempotent at which $W$ attains its maximum, so the components of $e$, which are multiples of $p$, $q$, and $\tau[p, q]$, are pairwise orthogonal by \eqref{eq:idemnorms} and span a $\tau$-stable subalgebra $\mathfrak{s}$ of Dynkin index $1$; hence $H(p, q) = 0$ and $p, q \in \mathfrak{s}$. Conversely, if $H(p, q) = 0$ and $p, q$ lie in such a subalgebra, then $F(p, q) = 1/h^\vee$ by \eqref{eq:sl2norm}.

label: lem:indexone
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:indexone}
A nonzero representation $\rho$ of a complex simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ has Dynkin index $\ell_{\rho} = 1$ if and only if, up to trivial summands, $\rho$ is the defining representation of $\mathfrak{sl}(n, \mathbb C)$, $n \geq 2$, or its dual, or the defining representation of $\mathfrak{sp}(2n, \mathbb C)$, $n \geq 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The index is additive under direct sums, takes positive integer values on nontrivial representations \cite[Theorem~2.2]{Dynkin-semisimplesubalgebras}, and vanishes on trivial ones. Hence a representation of index $1$ is the sum of an irreducible representation $V(\lambda)$ of index $1$ and trivial summands. By \cite[Theorem~2.5]{Dynkin-semisimplesubalgebras}, $\ell_{V(\lambda)} = \dim V(\lambda)\,(\lambda, \lambda + 2\delta)/\dim \mathfrak{g}$, where $2\delta = \sum_{\alpha \in \Phi^{+}}\alpha$. Let $\varpi_{1}, \dots, \varpi_{r}$ be the fundamental weights. If $\lambda = \lambda' + \varpi_{j}$ with $\lambda'$ dominant and nonzero, then $\dim V(\lambda) > \dim V(\varpi_{j})$ by the Weyl dimension formula, and $(\lambda, \lambda + 2\delta) - (\varpi_{j}, \varpi_{j} + 2\delta) = (\lambda', \lambda' + 2\varpi_{j} + 2\delta) > 0$, so $\ell_{V(\lambda)} > \ell_{V(\varpi_{j})} \geq 1$. Hence $\lambda$ is a fundamental weight with $\ell_{V(\lambda)} = 1$. By \cite[Proposition~2.6]{Laszlo-Sorger}, the index of every representation is divisible by $2$, $6$, $12$, or $60$ unless $\mathfrak{g}$ has type $A_{r}$ or $C_{r}$, and the fundamental weights of index $1$ are $\varpi_{1}$ and $\varpi_{r}$ for $A_{r}$ and $\varpi_{1}$ for $C_{r}$.

title: Lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{basic5}, the derivative of $\lVert [x, y]\rVert^{2}$ in the direction $(\dot{x}, \dot{y})$ is $2\operatorname{Re} H(Q(y)x, \dot{x}) + 2\operatorname{Re} H(Q(x)y, \dot{y})$, and the derivatives of $\lVert x\rVert^{2}\lVert y\rVert^{2}$ and of $\lVert x\rVert^{2}\lVert y\rVert^{2} - |H(x, y)|^{2}$ are $2\operatorname{Re} H(\lVert y\rVert^{2}x, \dot{x}) + 2\operatorname{Re} H(\lVert x\rVert^{2}y, \dot{y})$ and $2\operatorname{Re} H(\lVert y\rVert^{2}x - H(x, y)y, \dot{x}) + 2\operatorname{Re} H(\lVert x\rVert^{2}y - H(y, x)x, \dot{y})$. There follow \eqref{eq:F} and \eqref{eq:K}. 

If \eqref{eq:F} holds, then $F(x, y)\lVert y\rVert^{2}H(x, y) = H(Q(y)x, y) = H([y, x], [y, y]) = 0$. Let $z := \tau[x, y]$ and $t := \omega(x, y, z) = -\lVert [x, y]\rVert^{2}$, which is nonzero. Because $\tau$ is an automorphism, \eqref{eq:F} and $\lVert [x, y]\rVert^{2} = F(x, y)\lVert x\rVert^{2}\lVert y\rVert^{2}$ give $[y, z] = \tau[\tau y, [x, y]] = \tauQ(y)x = -(t/\lVert x\rVert^{2})\tau x$ and $[z, x] = -\tau[\tau x, [x, y]] = \tauQ(x)y = -(t/\lVert y\rVert^{2})\tau y$, while $[x, y] = \tau z = -(t/\lVert z\rVert^{2})\tau z$ because $\lVert z\rVert^{2} = -t$. So \eqref{eq:W} holds, and $W(x, y, z) = |t|^{2}/(\lVert x\rVert^{2}\lVert y\rVert^{2}\lVert z\rVert^{2}) = F(x, y)$. This completes the proof of \ref{critF}.

If $H(x, y) = 0$, then $\mathscr{K}(x, y) = F(x, y)$ and \eqref{eq:K} coincides with \eqref{eq:F}. The map $\mathscr{V}(\mathfrak{g}) \to \operatorname{Gr}(2, \mathfrak{g})$ is a surjective submersion along whose fibers $\mathscr{K}$ is constant by \eqref{eq:sectinvariance}, which proves \ref{corr3}.

Because $F$ and $W$ are invariant under rescaling their arguments, by Lemma \ref{thm:idem}\ref{idem1} to prove \ref{corr2} it suffices to suppose that $a \in \mathrm{Crit}^*(W)$ is a $\tau$-twisted idempotent $e \in \mathbb{Idem}_{\tau}(\mathfrak{g}^{3}, \circledcirc)$. By Lemma \ref{thm:idem}\ref{idem2}, 
\begin{align}\label{eq:corrcheck}
Q(e_{2})e_{1} = [\tau e_{2}, [e_{1}, e_{2}]] = \tfrac{1}{2}\tau[e_{2}, e_{3}] = \tfrac{1}{4}e_{1}, \qquad Q(e_{1})e_{2} = -[\tau e_{1}, [e_{1}, e_{2}]] = \tfrac{1}{2}\tau[e_{3}, e_{1}] = \tfrac{1}{4}e_{2},
\end{align}
and $F(e_{1}, e_{2})\lVert e_{1}\rVert^{2} = F(e_{1}, e_{2})\lVert e_{2}\rVert^{2} = \tfrac{1}{4}$ by \eqref{eq:idemnorms}, so, by \eqref{eq:corrcheck}, $(e_{1}, e_{2})$ satisfies \eqref{eq:F}; the same computation applies to $(e_{2}, e_{3})$ and $(e_{3}, e_{1})$. This proves \ref{corr2}.

\label{thm:sl2crit}
Let $\mathfrak{s} \subset \mathfrak{g}$ be a $\tau$-stable subalgebra isomorphic to $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$ and having Dynkin index $j$, and let $z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}$ be as in \eqref{eq:xirelations} of Lemma \ref{lem:sl2str}\ref{sl2a}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*), ref=(\arabic*)]
\item\label{sl2crit2} Every pair of nonzero $H$-orthogonal $x, y \in \mathfrak{s}$ lies in $\mathrm{Crit}^*(F)$, with $F(x, y) = 1/(jh^\vee)$.
\item\label{sl2crit1} Every $\sigma \in \operatorname{Gr}(2, \mathfrak{s})$ is a critical point of $\mathscr{K}$ on $\operatorname{Gr}(2, \mathfrak{g})$, with $\mathscr{K}(\sigma) = 1/(jh^\vee)$.
\item\label{sl2crit3} $e := \tfrac{1}{2}(z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3})$ is a $\tau$-twisted idempotent with $W(e) = 1/(jh^\vee)$ and $H(e, e) = \tfrac{3}{4}jh^\vee$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, by Lemma \ref{lem:lower}\ref{lower1}, for every subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}$ isomorphic to $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$, having Dynkin index $j$, the number $1/(jh^\vee)$ is a critical value of each of $F$, $\mathscr{K}$, and $W$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $(a, b, c)$ a cyclic permutation of $(1, 2, 3)$, $\mu_{b} + \mu_{c} = -\mu_{a}$ is a root, so $[\mathfrak{g}_{\mu_{b}}, \mathfrak{g}_{\mu_{c}}] = \mathfrak{g}_{-\mu_{a}}$ \cite[Proposition~8.4]{Humphreys}, which equals $\mathbb C\,\tau e_{a}$ by \eqref{eq:tauroot} and \ref{R2}. Moreover $C(e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}) = B([e_{1}, e_{2}], e_{3}) \neq 0$, because $[e_{1}, e_{2}]$ spans $\mathfrak{g}_{-\mu_{3}}$ and $B$ pairs $\mathfrak{g}_{-\mu_{3}}$ and $\mathfrak{g}_{\mu_{3}}$ nondegenerately. Lemma \ref{lem:critW} shows $(e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}) \in \mathrm{Crit}^*(W)$, which is \ref{tri1}.

For \ref{tri3}, if the $\mu_{a}$ are long and $a \neq b$, then $(\mu_{a} + \mu_{b}, \mu_{a} + \mu_{b}) \leq 2$ forces $(\mu_{a}, \mu_{b}) \leq -1$, so $(\mu_{a} - \mu_{b}, \mu_{a} - \mu_{b}) \geq 6$ and $\mu_{a} - \mu_{b} \notin \Phi$ by \ref{R1}. If the $\mu_{a}$ have a common squared length $\ell$, then $(\mu_{a}, \mu_{b}) = -\ell/2$ for $a \neq b$, because $\mu_{a} + \mu_{b} = -\mu_{c}$, so $(\mu_{a} - \mu_{b}, \mu_{a} - \mu_{b}) = 3\ell$, which is the squared length of a root only for short roots of $G_{2}$. The value in \ref{tri3} follows from \eqref{eq:trianglevalue} with $(\mu_{1}, \mu_{1}) = 2$, once \ref{tri2} is proved.

For \ref{tri2}, suppose $\mu_{a} - \mu_{b} \notin \Phi$ for $a \neq b$, and let $(a, b, c)$ be a cyclic permutation of $(1, 2, 3)$. The $\mu_{a}$-string through $\mu_{b}$ is $\mu_{b}, \mu_{b} + \mu_{a}$, because $\mu_{b} - \mu_{a} \notin \Phi$ and $\mu_{b} + 2\mu_{a} = \mu_{a} - \mu_{c} \notin \Phi$, so $\mu_{b}(\mu_{a}^{\vee}) = -1$ \cite[Proposition~8.4]{Humphreys}. By \ref{R2} and $t_{\mu_{a}} = (\mu_{a}, \mu_{a})\mu_{a}^{\vee}/(4h^\vee)$, the elements $X_{+} := e_{a}$ and $X_{-} := -4h^\vee\,\tau e_{a}/((\mu_{a}, \mu_{a})\lVert e_{a}\rVert^{2})$ satisfy $[X_{+}, X_{-}] = \mu_{a}^{\vee}$. Since $[X_{-}, e_{b}] \in \mathfrak{g}_{\mu_{b} - \mu_{a}} = 0$ and $[\mu_{a}^{\vee}, e_{b}] = -e_{b}$, the Jacobi identity gives $[X_{-}, [X_{+}, e_{b}]] = -[\mu_{a}^{\vee}, e_{b}] = e_{b}$, that is,
\begin{align}\label{eq:triangleQ}
Q(e_{a})e_{b} = -[\tau e_{a}, [e_{a}, e_{b}]] = \frac{(\mu_{a}, \mu_{a})\lVert e_{a}\rVert^{2}}{4h^\vee}\,e_{b}.
\end{align}
By \eqref{eq:triangleQ}, $F(e_{a}, e_{b}) = H(Q(e_{a})e_{b}, e_{b})/(\lVert e_{a}\rVert^{2}\lVert e_{b}\rVert^{2}) = (\mu_{a}, \mu_{a})/(4h^\vee)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:critFK}\ref{corr2} and the symmetry of $F$, $F(e_{a}, e_{b}) = W(e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3})$ for all $a \neq b$, so the $\mu_{a}$ have a common length and $W(e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}) = (\mu_{1}, \mu_{1})/(4h^\vee)$.

The space $\mathfrak{s}$ contains $t_{\mu_{3}} = -t_{\mu_{1}} - t_{\mu_{2}}$, and it is closed under brackets because $[\mathfrak{g}_{\mu_{a}}, \mathfrak{g}_{\mu_{b}}] = \mathfrak{g}_{-\mu_{c}}$, $[\mathfrak{g}_{-\mu_{a}}, \mathfrak{g}_{-\mu_{b}}] = \mathfrak{g}_{\mu_{c}}$, $[\mathfrak{g}_{\mu_{a}}, \mathfrak{g}_{-\mu_{b}}] \subset \mathfrak{g}_{\mu_{a} - \mu_{b}} = 0$ for $a \neq b$, and $[\mathfrak{g}_{\mu_{a}}, \mathfrak{g}_{-\mu_{a}}] = \mathbb C t_{\mu_{a}}$ by \ref{R2}. It is $\tau$-stable by \eqref{eq:tauroot}, because $t_{\mu} \in i\mathfrak{t}_{0}$ satisfies $\tau t_{\mu} = -t_{\mu}$; hence, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{thm:idem}\ref{idem3}, $\mathfrak{s}$ is reductive. Its center is trivial, because $B$ is nondegenerate on $\operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb C}\{t_{\mu_{1}}, t_{\mu_{2}}\}$, so no nonzero element of this space is annihilated by $\mu_{1}$ and $\mu_{2}$. Thus $\mathfrak{s}$ is semisimple of dimension $8$ with the $2$-dimensional Cartan subalgebra $\operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb C}\{t_{\mu_{1}}, t_{\mu_{2}}\}$, so $\mathfrak{s} \simeq \mathfrak{sl}(3, \mathbb C)$, all of whose roots are long. By \eqref{eq:dynkinpullback}, $(\,\cdot\,\,, \,\cdot\,\,)$ restricts to $j(\,\cdot\,\,, \,\cdot\,\,)_{\mathfrak{s}}$ on $\mathfrak{s}$, so the induced forms on the duals of the Cartan subalgebras satisfy $(\mu_{1}, \mu_{1}) = (\mu_{1}, \mu_{1})_{\mathfrak{s}}/j = 2/j$, which gives the second equality in \eqref{eq:trianglevalue}.

body_md:
\label{lem:indexbound}
Let $e \in \mathbb{Idem}_{\tau}(\mathfrak{g}^{3}, \circledcirc)$, and let $\mu$ run over the eigenvalues of $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)$ on $U^{\perp}_{e}$, counted with real multiplicity. Then the coindex, nullity, and index of $[e]$ are $\#\{\mu > \tfrac{1}{2}\}$, $\#\{\mu = \tfrac{1}{2}\}$, and $\#\{\mu < \tfrac{1}{2}\} \geq D$, with equality in the last if and only if $\lvert \tau\mathsf{L}(e)b\rvert \geq \tfrac{1}{2}\lvert b\rvert$ for all $b \in U^{\perp}_{e}$. title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma \ref{hess2}, $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)$ is self-adjoint on $U^{\perp}_{e}$, so \eqref{eq:hessR} gives the counts. If $\operatorname{Hess} W_{e}$ is positive semidefinite on a subspace $V \subset U^{\perp}_{e}$, then by \eqref{eq:hessJ} it is negative definite on $JV$, so the index is at least $\dim_{\mathbb R}V$. Taking $V$ maximal, so that $\dim_{\mathbb R}V$ is $\dim_{\mathbb R}U^{\perp}_{e}$ minus the index, shows that the index is at least $\tfrac{1}{2}\dim_{\mathbb R}U^{\perp}_{e} = D$. Since $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)$ anticommutes with $J$, its eigenvalues on $U^{\perp}_{e}$ come in pairs $\pm\mu$, with $\mu \geq 0$ and eigenvectors $b$ and $Jb$, on which $\operatorname{Hess} W_{e}$ takes the values $16W(e)^{2}(\pm\mu - \tfrac{1}{2})\lvert b\rvert^{2}$; such a pair contributes two negative directions if $\mu < \tfrac{1}{2}$ and one otherwise, which gives the equality statement.

label: eq:casimirM
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A_{l} := \operatorname{ad}(z_{l})$ for $l \in \{1, 2, 3\}$. These operators are skew-Hermitian, commute with $\tau$, and satisfy $[A_{1}, A_{2}] = A_{3}$, $[A_{2}, A_{3}] = A_{1}$, $[A_{3}, A_{1}] = A_{2}$ by \eqref{eq:xirelations}. Since $e = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{3}z_{l} \otimes \mathsf{c}_{l}$, \eqref{eq:nahmtensor} gives $\mathsf{L}(e) = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{3}A_{l} \otimes T_{l} = \tfrac{1}{2}M$, so $\tau\mathsf{L}(e) = \tfrac{1}{2}\tau M$. The operators $T_{l}$ are the adjoint operators of $(\mathbb C^{3}, \times)$, so $[T_{1}, T_{2}] = T_{3}$, $[T_{2}, T_{3}] = T_{1}$, and $[T_{3}, T_{1}] = T_{2}$. Each $A_{l} \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes T_{l}$ is skew-Hermitian, and these operators satisfy the relations of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, whose Casimir $\sum_{l=1}^{3}(A_{l} \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes T_{l})^{2}$ acts on the irreducible module $V(q)$ as $-\tfrac{1}{4}q(q+2)$. Expanding the square shows
\begin{align}\label{eq:casimirM}
M = \tfrac{1}{2}\Big(\sum_{l=1}^{3}(A_{l} \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes T_{l})^{2} - \sum_{l=1}^{3}A_{l}^{2}\otimes 1 - 1 \otimes \sum_{l=1}^{3}T_{l}^{2}\Big).
\end{align}
Since $\sum_{l=1}^{3}A_{l}^{2} = -\tfrac{1}{4}d(d+2)$ on $V(d)$ and $\sum_{l=1}^{3}T_{l}^{2} = -2$, by \eqref{eq:casimirM} the operator $M$ acts on the summand $V(q)$ of $V(d) \otimes \mathbb C^{3}$ as $\tfrac{1}{2}\big(-\tfrac{1}{4}q(q+2) + \tfrac{1}{4}d(d+2) + 2\big)$, which is $-\tfrac{d}{2}$, $1$, $\tfrac{d}{2}+1$ for $q = d+2, d, d-2$. $M$ is Hermitian because the $A_{l}$ and $T_{l}$ are skew, and commutes with $\tau$ because $\tau$ commutes with the $A_{l}$ and the $T_{l}$ are real. An eigenspace $E_{m}$ of $M$ is therefore $\tau$-stable, $E_{m} = E_{m}^{\tau} \oplus iE_{m}^{\tau}$ with $E_{m}^{\tau}$ the fixed points of $\tau$, and $\tfrac{1}{2}\tau M$ acts as $\tfrac{m}{2}$ on $E_{m}^{\tau}$ and as $-\tfrac{m}{2}$ on $iE_{m}^{\tau}$. This proves \ref{morse1}.

For \ref{morse2}, $\mathfrak{g}^{3} = (\mathfrak{s} \otimes \mathbb C^{3}) \oplus (\mathfrak{s}^{\perp}\otimes \mathbb C^{3})$ is an $H$-orthogonal decomposition into $M$-invariant subspaces, and $U_{e} \subset \mathfrak{s} \otimes \mathbb C^{3}$, so $U^{\perp}_{e} = (U^{\perp}_{e} \cap (\mathfrak{s} \otimes \mathbb C^{3})) \oplus (\mathfrak{s}^{\perp}\otimes \mathbb C^{3})$. By \eqref{eq:hessR} and \ref{morse1}, each eigenspace $E_{m}$ of $M$ contained in $U^{\perp}_{e}$ contributes eigenvalues $16W(e)^{2}(\tfrac{|m|}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2})$ and $16W(e)^{2}(-\tfrac{|m|}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2})$, each with real multiplicity $\dim_{\mathbb C}E_{m}$. Hence $E_{m}$ contributes $\dim_{\mathbb C}E_{m}$ to the index, and in addition $\dim_{\mathbb C}E_{m}$ to the coindex if $|m| > 1$, to the nullity if $|m| = 1$, and to the index if $|m| < 1$. Identify $\mathfrak{s} \otimes \mathbb C^{3}$ with the $3\times 3$ complex matrices via $z_{a} \otimes \mathsf{c}_{b} \mapsto E_{ab}$. Then $A_{l}$ acts on $\mathfrak{s}$ as $T_{l}$, the decomposition $V(2) \otimes \mathbb C^{3} = V(4) \oplus V(2) \oplus V(0)$ is the decomposition into symmetric trace-free, antisymmetric, and scalar matrices, with $M$-eigenvalues $-1$, $1$, $2$, and $U_{e}$ is the space of complex diagonal matrices. Hence $U^{\perp}_{e} \cap (\mathfrak{s} \otimes \mathbb C^{3})$, the matrices with vanishing diagonal, lies in the sum of the eigenspaces with $|m| = 1$ and has complex dimension $6$, contributing $6$ to the nullity and $6$ to the index. The summands of \eqref{eq:sperpdecomp} contribute as follows: $V(0)\otimes\mathbb C^{3}$, with $m = 0$, contributes index $6$; $V(1)\otimes\mathbb C^{3} = V(3) \oplus V(1)$, with $m = -\tfrac{1}{2}, 1$, contributes nullity $2$ and index $8 + 2 = 10$; $V(2)\otimes\mathbb C^{3}$, with $m = -1, 1, 2$, contributes coindex $1$, nullity $5 + 3 = 8$, and index $9$; and for $d \geq 3$, $V(d)\otimes\mathbb C^{3}$, with $m = -\tfrac{d}{2}, 1, \tfrac{d}{2}+1$, contributes coindex $(d+3) + (d-1) = 2d+2$, nullity $d+1$, and index $3(d+1)$. Summing gives the coindex and nullity in \eqref{eq:morseindex}, and the index $6 + 6n_{0} + 10n_{1} + 9n_{2} + \sum_{d \geq 3}3(d+1)n_{d}$, which equals $D + 3n_{0} + 4n_{1}$ because $\dim_{\mathbb C}\mathfrak{g} = 3 + n_{0} + 2n_{1} + 3n_{2} + \sum_{d \geq 3}(d+1)n_{d}$.

For \ref{morse3}, let $(e_{+}, e_{-}, h)$ be an $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$-triple spanning $\mathfrak{s}$. The Hessian is negative semidefinite if and only if the coindex vanishes, which by \eqref{eq:morseindex} happens if and only if $n_{d} = 0$ for $d \geq 2$, that is, if and only if the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{ad}(h)$ on $\mathfrak{s}^{\perp}$ lie in $\{0, \pm 1\}$. If $j = 1$, then $h$ is conjugate to $\theta^{\vee}$ by Lemma \ref{lem:Bh}, and by \ref{R1} and the equality case of \eqref{eq:CSh} the only roots taking the value $\pm 2$ on $\theta^{\vee}$ are $\pm\theta$ and no root takes a larger value, so the condition holds. Conversely, suppose the condition holds, and, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:Bh}, conjugate $h$ to a dominant element of the real span of the coroots in $\mathfrak{h}$. Then $2$ is the largest eigenvalue of $\operatorname{ad}(h)$ and its eigenspace is $\mathbb C e_{+}$, and similarly for $-2$ and $\mathbb C e_{-}$. Since $\theta(h) \geq 2$ by the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:Bh}, $\theta(h) = 2$ and $\mathfrak{g}_{\theta} = \mathbb C e_{+}$; likewise $\mathfrak{g}_{-\theta} = \mathbb C e_{-}$, so $h = [e_{+}, e_{-}] \in \mathbb C t_{\theta}$ by \ref{R2}, and $\theta(h) = 2$ forces $h = \theta^{\vee}$, so $j = 1$.

For \ref{morse4}, by \eqref{eq:morseindex}, $\operatorname{ind} = D$ if and only if $n_{0} = n_{1} = 0$. The centralizer $\mathfrak{z}_{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathfrak{s})$ is the isotypic component $n_{0}V(0)$, so $n_{0} = \dim_{\mathbb C}\mathfrak{z}_{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathfrak{s})$. A subalgebra isomorphic to $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$ is distinguished if and only if its centralizer contains no nonzero semisimple element, which for the reductive Lie algebra $\mathfrak{z}_{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathfrak{s})$ means $\mathfrak{z}_{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathfrak{s}) = 0$; and distinguished subalgebras are even, so $n_{0} = 0$ forces $n_{1} = 0$ \cite[Section~8.2]{Collingwood-McGovern}. The principal subalgebra is distinguished.

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{rot1} The first claims hold because $R$ acts on the second factor of $\mathfrak{g} \otimes \mathbb C^{3}$ unitarily with respect to $u \cdot \bar{v}$, while $\tau$ is $\tau$ on $\mathfrak{g}$ tensored with complex conjugation of $\mathbb C^{3}$. By \eqref{eq:nahmtensor} and \eqref{eq:crossequivariance}, $(Ra) \circledcirc (Rb) = \det(R)(R^{t})^{-1}(a \circledcirc b)$ for pure tensors $a$ and $b$, hence for all $a, b \in \mathfrak{g}^{3}$, which is \eqref{eq:rotation} because $(R^{t})^{-1} = \bar{R}$ for unitary $R$. If $\det R = 1$, then, by \eqref{eq:rotation}, $(Re) \circledcirc (Re) = \bar{R}(e \circledcirc e) = \bar{R}\tau e = \tau(Re)$ and $\tau\mathsf{L}(Re)Rb = \tau\bar{R}(e \circledcirc b) = R\tau(e \circledcirc b) = R\,\tau\mathsf{L}(e)b$.

\ref{rot2} Let $e' \in\mathbb{Idem}_{\tau}(\mathfrak{g}^{3}, \circledcirc)$ be a nonzero $\tau$-twisted idempotent with components in $\mathfrak{s}$, and put $\beta := jh^\vee$. By Lemma \ref{thm:idem}\ref{idem2}, its components are pairwise $H$-orthogonal of a common norm and $F(e'_{1}, e'_{2}) = W(e') = 3/(4H(e', e'))$, while $F(e'_{1}, e'_{2}) = 1/\beta$ by \eqref{eq:sl2norm}; so $H(e'_{i}, e'_{p}) = \tfrac{\beta}{4}\delta_{ip}$ for $i, p \in \{1, 2, 3\}$. Write $e'_{i} = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{m=1}^{3}R_{im}z_{m}$ for $i \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, that is, $e' = Re$. Since $H(z_{l}, z_{m}) = \beta\delta_{lm}$ by \eqref{eq:xirelations}, also $H(e'_{i}, e'_{p}) = \tfrac{\beta}{4}(RR^{\dagger})_{ip}$, so $R$ is unitary. By \eqref{eq:rotation}, $\tau e' = e' \circledcirc e' = \det(R)\bar{R}\tau e$, while $\tau e' = \tau Re = \bar{R}\tau e$, so $\det R = 1$. Uniqueness holds because $z_{1}, z_{2}, z_{3}$ is a basis of $\mathfrak{s}$.

\ref{rot3} Let $e' = Re$ with $R \in SU(3)$, as in \ref{rot2}, so $W(e') = W(e)$. By \ref{rot1}, $\tau\mathsf{L}(e') = R\,\tau\mathsf{L}(e)R^{-1}$, so $\tau\mathsf{L}(e')$ and $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)$ have the same spectrum on $\mathfrak{s}\otimes\mathbb C^{3}$ and on $\mathfrak{s}^{\perp}\otimes\mathbb C^{3}$. Write $U_{e'}$ and $U^{\perp}_{e'}$ for the spaces \eqref{eq:UR} of $e'$. By \eqref{idem4} in the proof of Lemma \ref{hess2}, $\tau\mathsf{L}(e')$ acts on $\operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb R}\{\hat{e}'_{i}: i \in \{1, 2, 3\}\}$ with eigenvalues $1, -\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}$, and so, by the anticommutation with $J$, on the image of this space under $J$ with eigenvalues $-1, \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}$; the same holds for $e$. Since $U_{e'} \subset \mathfrak{s} \otimes \mathbb C^{3}$ and $U^{\perp}_{e'} = (U^{\perp}_{e'} \cap (\mathfrak{s}\otimes\mathbb C^{3})) \oplus (\mathfrak{s}^{\perp}\otimes\mathbb C^{3})$, and likewise for $e$, the operators $\tau\mathsf{L}(e')$ on $U^{\perp}_{e'}$ and $\tau\mathsf{L}(e)$ on $U^{\perp}_{e}$ have the same spectrum. By \eqref{eq:hessR}, the coindex, nullity, and index of $[e']$ and $[e]$ coincide.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:morsebott}
Let $\mathfrak{M} \subset \mathcal{P}$ be the set of maximum points of $W$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*), ref=(\arabic*)]
\item\label{mb1} $G_{0}$ acts transitively on $\mathcal{S}$, so $\mathcal{S} = G_{0}/N$ with $N := \{g \in G_{0}: \operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak{s}_{\theta} = \mathfrak{s}_{\theta}\}$, a compact manifold of real dimension $2n_{1}$.
\item\label{mb2} The map $[a] \mapsto \operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb C}\{a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\}$ is a smooth fiber bundle $\mathfrak{M} \to \mathcal{S}$ whose fiber over $\mathfrak{s}$ is the manifold of pairs $([a_{1}], [a_{2}])$ of $H$-orthogonal lines in $\mathfrak{s} \simeq \mathbb C^{3}$, that is, the manifold of complete flags in $\mathbb C^{3}$, which is $SU(3)/T^{2}$ with $T^{2}$ the maximal torus. In particular $\mathfrak{M}$ is a compact connected submanifold of $\mathcal{P}$ of real dimension $6 + 2n_{1}$.
\item\label{mb3} $\mathfrak{M}$ is a nondegenerate critical manifold of $W$ in the sense of Bott \cite{Bott-nondegenerate}: at every point of $\mathfrak{M}$, the kernel of the Hessian of $W$ on $\mathcal{P}$ is the tangent space of $\mathfrak{M}$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{mb1} Transitivity is Lemma \ref{lem:lower}\ref{lower3}. The Lie algebra of $N$ is the normalizer of $\mathfrak{s}_{\theta} \cap \mathfrak{g}_{0}$ in $\mathfrak{g}_{0}$, which is $(\mathfrak{s}_{\theta} \cap \mathfrak{g}_{0}) \oplus \mathfrak{z}_{\mathfrak{g}_{0}}(\mathfrak{s}_{\theta} \cap \mathfrak{g}_{0})$ because every derivation of a semisimple Lie algebra is inner. Since $\mathfrak{z}_{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathfrak{s}_{\theta}) = n_{0}V(0)$ is $\tau$-stable, $\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathcal{S} = \dim_{\mathbb R}\mathfrak{g}_{0} - 3 - n_{0} = \dim_{\mathbb C}\mathfrak{g} - 3 - n_{0} = 2n_{1}$.

\ref{mb2} By Theorem \ref{thm:A} and Lemma \ref{fkwmaxlemma}\ref{fkw2}, $[a] \in \mathfrak{M}$ if and only if $F(a_{1}, a_{2}) = 1/h^\vee$ and $a_{3} \in \mathbb C\,\tau[a_{1}, a_{2}]$, that is, if and only if $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ are $H$-orthogonal elements of some $\mathfrak{s} \in \mathcal{S}$ and $a_{3} \in \mathbb C\,\tau[a_{1}, a_{2}]$. In that case $a_{3} \in \mathfrak{s}$, and $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}$ are pairwise $H$-orthogonal by Lemma \ref{thm:idem}, so $\mathfrak{s} = \operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb C}\{a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\}$ is determined by $[a]$. Let $\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}$ be the set of triples $(\mathfrak{s}, \ell_{1}, \ell_{2})$ with $\mathfrak{s} \in \mathcal{S}$ and $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}$ $H$-orthogonal lines in $\mathfrak{s}$; it is the bundle $G_{0} \times_{N} \mathcal{F}$ associated with $G_{0} \to \mathcal{S}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the manifold of pairs of $H$-orthogonal lines in $\mathfrak{s}_{\theta}$, of real dimension $6$, on which $N$ acts through $\operatorname{Ad}$. The map $\Psi:\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}} \to \mathcal{P}$, $(\mathfrak{s}, \ell_{1}, \ell_{2}) \mapsto (\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \tau[\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}])$, is therefore a smooth $G_{0}$-equivariant bijection onto $\mathfrak{M}$. It restricts on each fiber to an embedding into $\mathbb{P}(\mathfrak{s})^{3}$, and its composition with the map $[a] \mapsto \operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb C}\{a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\}$ to the Grassmannian of $3$-planes in $\mathfrak{g}$, which is smooth on the triples of linearly independent lines, is the bundle projection onto the orbit $\mathcal{S}$; hence the differential of $\Psi$ is injective. Being an injective immersion of a compact connected manifold, $\Psi$ is an embedding.

\ref{mb3} Since $\mathfrak{M}$ consists of critical points, its tangent space is contained in the kernel of the Hessian. Let $[a] \in \mathfrak{M}$. By Lemma \ref{thm:idem}\ref{idem1}, $[a] = [e']$ for a $\tau$-twisted idempotent $e' \in \mathbb{Idem}_{\tau}(\mathfrak{g}^{3}, \circledcirc)$, whose components lie in some $\mathfrak{s} \in \mathcal{S}$ by \ref{mb2}. By Lemma \ref{lem:rotation}\ref{rot3} and Theorem \ref{thm:morse}\ref{morse2} with $n_{d} = 0$ for $d \geq 2$, the nullity at $[a]$ is $6 + 2n_{1} = \dim_{\mathbb R}\mathfrak{M}$.

label: rem:minimalvalue
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:minimalvalue}
Among the critical points of Lemma \ref{thm:sl2crit}, the smallest critical value is $1/(jh^\vee)$ for the largest Dynkin index $j$ of a subalgebra isomorphic to $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb C)$, which is attained exactly by the principal subalgebra, for which $j = 2(\rho^{\vee}, \rho^{\vee})$, where $\rho^{\vee}$ is half the sum of the positive coroots. Indeed, the dominant characteristic $h$ of any such subalgebra satisfies $\alpha_{i}(h) \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ for the simple roots $\alpha_{i}$, $i \in \{1, \dots, \operatorname{rk}\mathfrak{g}\}$ \cite[Section~3.5]{Collingwood-McGovern}, so $h = \sum_{i=1}^{\operatorname{rk}\mathfrak{g}}c_{i}\varpi_{i}^{\vee}$ with $0 \leq c_{i} \leq 2$ in terms of the fundamental coweights $\varpi_{i}^{\vee}$, the basis dual to the simple roots, whose pairwise inner products are positive because the inverse Cartan matrix has positive entries; since $2\rho^{\vee} = \sum_{i=1}^{\operatorname{rk}\mathfrak{g}}2\varpi_{i}^{\vee}$, $(h, h) \leq (2\rho^{\vee}, 2\rho^{\vee})$ with equality if and only if $c_{i} = 2$ for all $i$ (see also \cite{Panyushev-dynkinindex}). By Theorem \ref{thm:morse}\ref{morse4}, the index at this point is $D$, the smallest value permitted by Lemma \ref{lem:indexbound}. The critical points of Lemma \ref{thm:roottriangle} show that not all critical points are of the type of Lemma \ref{thm:sl2crit}. It is not known whether $1/(2(\rho^{\vee}, \rho^{\vee})h^\vee)$ is the infimum of the nonzero critical values of $W$, nor whether the index at a critical point realizing this infimum must equal $D$. On $\operatorname{Gr}(2, \mathfrak{g}_{0})$ the nonzero critical values of $\mathscr{K}$ are exactly the numbers $1/(jh^\vee)$ (Remark \ref{rem:meshcheryakov}), so there the infimum is $1/(2(\rho^{\vee}, \rho^{\vee})h^\vee)$, attained exactly on the planes in principal subalgebras.
